messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Film Director
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Distraction: I distract myself with something else
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-two when a construction crane collapsed on the set of his latest film. He had been standing near the edge of the soundstage, reviewing footage on a monitor, when a sudden metallic shriek cut through the ambient noise—a sound he would later describe as the world tearing open. The crane's arm fell in slow motion and then all at once, crushing the lighting rig beside him. He felt the percussion of impact through his chest, saw the shower of sparks, tasted metal and dust. For three seconds he could not move. Then his assistant was pulling him backward, and he was on the ground, gasping, certain he was dying. The hospital confirmed what the emergency room doctor told him: he had escaped by less than a meter. A fracture in his left radius, lacerations, but alive. The crane operator had suffered a catastrophic mechanical failure—nothing Marcus could have foreseen or prevented. And yet, for the past eighteen months, that distinction had become increasingly difficult to hold.

The nightmares began within a week. Marcus would wake at two or three in the morning with his heart hammering, the image of the falling crane suspended in perfect, merciless clarity behind his eyes. The memory had a photographic quality that unnerved him—not a narrative he could tell but a series of stills: the monitor screen, the shadow crossing the floor, the arc of metal against the grid lights. When he tried to describe it to his partner, David, the words felt inadequate, almost absurd. How could he explain the way the memory didn't feel like something that had happened but something that was still happening, replayed in his nervous system every time a door slammed or a truck rumbled past their Brooklyn brownstone?

Within weeks, Marcus had begun to avoid the soundstage entirely. He told the studio he needed time to recover, that he would direct remotely. The lie felt safer than the truth: that stepping back into that space—even in daylight, even with the crane removed—triggered a cascade of panic that left him shaking for hours afterward. He filled his days with smaller distractions. He rewatched old films, scrolled through social media, organized his archive of photographs from past productions. Anything to keep his mind occupied, to prevent it from drifting back to those three seconds. The distraction worked, but only in the moment. Each time he looked away, the weight of what he was avoiding seemed to grow heavier.

What troubled Marcus most deeply was the person he had become. He had always prided himself on his composure under pressure, his ability to make split-second decisions with confidence. Now he found himself jumping at the sound of a dropped plate, his entire body flooding with adrenaline at a car horn outside the window. He was hypervigilant in ways he couldn't control—constantly scanning for threat, listening for the next unexpected sound that might herald disaster. The vividness of his memories, their intrusive visual clarity, convinced him that his reactions were evidence of fundamental weakness. A stronger person would have moved past this by now. A competent director, a capable man, would not be undone by a sound. This belief—that his persistent fear and startle response revealed him to be a lousy coper, fundamentally inadequate—drove him deeper into avoidance. He stopped attending industry events, declined social invitations, worked only on projects he could manage from home. Each time he avoided a situation, he told himself it was temporary, a necessary reprieve. But the reprieve never came. Instead, the avoidance seemed to amplify his sense of threat. The world outside his apartment felt increasingly dangerous, unpredictable. Sounds that most people would barely register—the beep of a delivery truck, the crash of construction work several blocks away—sent him into a state of acute vigilance, his body braced for impact.

The hyperalertness fed back into his memory in ways Marcus was only beginning to recognize. When he heard a loud noise, the vividness of his traumatic memory spiked, as if the sound had opened a door directly into that moment on the soundstage. His threat detection system, now permanently sensitized, interpreted the memory's clarity as confirmation that danger was imminent and inescapable. This cycle of threat and memory began to feel like proof of his inadequacy, evidence that he was broken in some irreparable way. By the time he contacted his therapist, Marcus had withdrawn from most of his life. David had grown quiet and distant, hurt by the rejection that Marcus's avoidance had created. Work had become a phantom thing—projects he managed through email, his creative voice reduced to typed comments on scripts he could barely focus on. He had come to believe that the man he used to be—decisive, engaged, unafraid—was gone, replaced by someone he no longer recognized. What he wanted most was to feel safe in his own body again. What he feared most was that the person he had been before the crane fell would never come back.
